title: Undercover – a primal heuristic for MINLP based on sub-MIPs generated by set covering
contribution: Undercover, a root-node start heuristic for MINLP that fixes a minimum cover (computed by a set covering program) to relaxation values so that the rest is a MIP; on 33 MINLPLib MIQCPs it finds solutions on 21 instances, 7 of them missed by the root heuristics of SCIP, BARON and Couenne, in under 0.2 s of its own time except on one instance.
problem_entry: MINLP had few general-purpose primal heuristics, and for several practical MIQCPs fixing a small set of variables already linearizes the problem (pp. 1–2, 4).
key_idea: Fix an x*-cover to values from a relaxation and solve the sub-MIP, each of whose solutions is MINLP-feasible; the fixing targets nonlinearity, not integrality, so as few variables as possible are fixed (pp. 1–3).
assumptions: MINLP (22.1) with linear objective; MIQCPs with symmetric, possibly indefinite A_i; fixing values from SCIP's LP outer approximation, unavailable when the root LP is unbounded; 33 MINLPLib MIQCPs with named exclusions (pp. 2, 4, 6–7).
proof_devices: Cover of a quadratic function iff one endpoint of each nonzero Q_uv is fixed: covering program (22.3)–(22.5) and Lemma 22.6 (pp. 4–5)
Remark 22.7: an optimisation version of 2-SAT, hence polynomial, but solved by a general MIP solver in a fraction of a second (p. 5)
Sufficient cover conditions for monomials; x*-cover versus global cover example (p. 5, fn. 1)
Remark 22.3: a minimum cover only approximates a dimension-wise largest sub-MIP (p. 3)
Fix-and-propagate with closest-bound repair and one-level backtracking over listed alternative values (p. 5, fn. 3)
experiments: SCIP 1.2.0.4 with CPLEX 12.1 and Ipopt 3.7; node limit 1 for UC (other heuristics off, no cuts, node limit 500 for covering problem and sub-MIP), SCIP default (ten root heuristics), BARON and Couenne; 33 MINLPLib MIQCPs; UC feasible on 21 (SCIP 14, BARON 15, Couenne 9; 7 by UC alone); better/equal/worse against SCIP 1/1/8, BARON 4/4/3, Couenne 1/2/3; UC time under 0.2 s except one instance (1.1 s); 10 of 14 infeasible sub-MIPs caught in fix-and-propagate; no hardware stated (pp. 6–8).
positioning: Carries the MIP large-neighbourhood paradigm (Local Branching, RINS, DINS, RENS) to MINLP; fix-and-propagate after Fischetti and Salvagnin's feasibility pump 2.0; NLP postprocessing after the QCP local search of Berthold, Heinz and Vigerske; links to bilinear programming in global optimization (pp. 1, 4–6).
writing: Hedged ('seems most promising', 'seem to confirm our expectation', 'seems to be a fast start heuristic'); remarks concede what a minimum cover does not give; the unfavourable quality counts are printed (pp. 1, 3, 8).
limits_future: No fixing values when the root LP is unbounded; solution quality mostly below SCIP's root heuristics; the §4 variants only partly implemented. Future: implement and test them, take fixing values from NLP relaxations (pp. 7–8).

method_links.note: matched by stage, not by features: all solvers stopped after the root and compared as root heuristics, not complete solvers; UC runs alone against SCIP's ten default root heuristics; the unflattering pairwise counts are printed
weak: prints where the heuristic cannot run (unbounded root LP on the nuclear instances), its quality losses and its unimplemented variants

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the nonlinear part is reduced to a sub-MIP so that the full strength of state-of-the-art MIP solving applies; recurs in S075, S030 and S054 (group-level)

transferable: To find the fewest variables whose fixing linearizes a quadratic system, solve a vertex-cover program over the nonzero quadratic terms (squares fixed, one endpoint of each bilinear term); if the MIP solver handles it in a fraction of a second, skip the special-case algorithm (pp. 4–5)

Fix one variable at a time and propagate after each fixing; move a value that left its domain to the closest bound; on infeasibility undo the last fixing and try a short list of alternatives (finite bounds, midpoints to them, zero, twice the value) (p. 5, fn. 3)

Evaluate a start heuristic against the other solvers' root-node heuristics only (node limit 1 everywhere) and report solutions found, pairwise better/equal/worse counts on common instances, and time (pp. 6–8)

quotes.text: Thus our heuristic will aim at fixing as few variables as possible to obtain as large a linear subproblem as possible.
We note that in 10 out of the 14 cases where the resulting sub-MIP was infeasible, the infeasibility was already detected during the fix-and-propagate stage.

title: Extending SCIP for solving MIQCPs
contribution: A poster on SCIP constraint handlers for quadratic, second-order cone and (experimentally) convex nonlinear constraints plus three large-neighbourhood heuristics, with a comparison against BARON, Couenne, CPLEX, LINDOglobal, Mosek and convex MINLP solvers on four public test sets.
problem_entry: Show how a CIP framework can be extended into a competitive MIQCP solver, so that existing MIP and CP technology handles the linear and discrete parts (p. 1).
key_idea: Constraint handlers with presolve reformulations, linearizations and termwise underestimators, interval propagation and enforcement after integrality, plus Fix-and-NLP, Fix-and-MINLP (RENS) and Fix-and-MIP (Undercover) heuristics, inside SCIP's LP-based branch and bound (pp. 2–4).
assumptions: MIQCPs including nonconvex ones, MIQPs, SOC portfolio problems, convex MINLPs; 25 Mittelmann MIQPs, 22 MICPs, 60 general MIQCPs (42 MINLPLib, 6 clay, 12 truss), 47 convex MINLPs from Bonami, Kılınç and Linderoth (pp. 4, 7–8).
proof_devices: Quadratic constraints enforced with lower priority than integrality, so spatial branching only at integer-feasible LP solutions (p. 3)
Presolve reformulations: binary×linear linearization, SOC detection, division reformulation of ℓ ≤ xy ≤ u for sign-definite y, eigenvalue convexity check (p. 2)
Termwise underestimation by linearization, secant or McCormick; SOC constraints enforced by gradient cuts only (pp. 2–3)
experiments: SCIP 1.2.0.7 (CPLEX 11.2.1, Ipopt 3.8) against BARON 9.0.2, Couenne 0.3, CPLEX 12.1, LINDOglobal 6.0.1 (limited licence), Mosek 6.0.0.55 and, for convex MINLPs, AlphaECP, BONMIN (BB, QG, Hyb), DICOPT, SBB; 1 h, gap 10^-4, feasibility 10^-6, Core2 Duo 2.5 GHz; non-default options listed; performance profiles on the 80 MIQCPs where at least two solvers took over 10 s and the licence allowed; per-instance tables (pp. 4–5, 7–15).
positioning: Places SCIP among MIP-based extensions to MINLP (FilMINT, BONMIN, Couenne) and CP–MIP integration (CIP); reuses McCormick underestimators, Domes–Neumaier propagation and the pseudocost spatial branching of Belotti et al. (pp. 1–3).
writing: A descriptive poster abstract without conclusion; the profiles are shown without a stated claim; a null result is reported in one sentence (pp. 3–5).
limits_future: Convex nonlinear support is experimental; no conclusion or future work is stated (pp. 1, 3–5).

method_links.note: a written inclusion rule for the profile (at least two solvers above 10 s, within the licence limit) and a column marking the profile instances; it filters an assembled collection for one figure, and exclusions are not counted

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: build MINLP on mature MIP machinery
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: a CIP/MIP framework is extended so that existing MIP and CP technology handles the linear and discrete parts

transferable: Enforce nonlinear constraints after integrality, so that spatial branching only meets LP solutions whose integer variables are integral (p. 3)

Before drawing a performance profile, filter trivial instances by a written rule (at least two solvers need more than 10 s) and mark in the per-instance table which instances entered the profile (pp. 4, 13)
coauthors: Timo Berthold, Stefan Heinz (ZIB), Stefan Vigerske (HU Berlin); the work list also names T. Koch, who is not on the file's byline (p. 1)

We also experimented with adding a linear outer-approximation of the SOC as suggested in [5] during presolve, but did not observe a computational benefit for the instances in our testset.

title: On the computational impact of MIQCP solver components
contribution: A component study of SCIP on 86 public MIQCPs: eleven settings that disable or simplify one component each, with relevant and control groups; all components help, the nonlinear ones most, while MILP and CP components act below their MILP effect.
problem_entry: Solver performance depends on its components and their interplay, and SCIP's plug-in architecture allows measuring each component on MIQCPs (p. 3).
key_idea: Ablate one component at a time against the default, MILP components included, with relevant/control groups for components that act only on a subset (p. 5).
assumptions: MIQCPs with possibly indefinite A_j; 86 public instances from clay/SLay, Mittelmann MIQPs, portfolio, truss, uflquad and MINLPLib (pp. 3, 5, 8–9).
proof_devices: SCIP's MIQCP components as ablated: binary-product reformulation, SOC detection, eigenvalue convexity check, termwise underestimators, interval propagation (pp. 4–5)
Conflict analysis on the linear part only; hybrid branching for integers and pseudocost spatial branching only at integer-feasible points (p. 5)
experiments: Xeon 5150 2.66 GHz; SCIP 1.2.1.1, CPLEX 12.1.0, Ipopt 3.8.1, LAPACK 3.1.0; optimality tolerance 0, feasibility 10^-6, 1 h, 4 GB; default solves 55 of 86; per setting: solved difference, counts of more than 10% faster or slower, bounds at termination for timeouts, shifted geometric means of time, nodes and time to first and optimal solution (shift not stated); nonlinear separation off −19 solved and +140% time; SOC upgrades off −8 of 12 relevant and +1098%; heuristics off +347% time to first solution (pp. 5–6).
positioning: Builds on the SCIP MIQCP extension of Berthold, Heinz and Vigerske and on Achterberg's CIP framework; other MINLP and MIQCP solvers appear only as context (pp. 3–5).
writing: Plain report style; the conclusion generalizes ('All 11 features proved to be beneficial'); a surprise is reported but not explained; the text lists ten of the eleven settings and leaves one citation unresolved ('[?]') (pp. 4–7).
limits_future: Nonlinear components act on small subsets; MILP and CP techniques below their potential, for conflict analysis probably a theoretical gap; one solver only, the same study for other solvers suggested (pp. 6–7).

method_links.note: gaps printed with a suspected cause: quadratic constraints outside conflict analysis, MILP and CP techniques below their MILP effect, a theoretical gap for conflict analysis, a single solver

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: for a component that acts only on some instances, report the relevant group and a control group expected to show no change; again in S028
the text names ten settings for 11 alternative settings (conflict analysis only in Table 1); an unresolved citation [?]

transferable: Ablate a nonlinear solver one component at a time against its default, including the classical MILP components (presolve, cuts, conflict analysis), and keep all rows in one table (pp. 5–6)
For a feature that acts only on some instances, report the affected group and a control group; a change in the control group exposes noise or side effects (p. 5)
coauthors: Timo Berthold, Stefan Heinz (ZIB), Stefan Vigerske (HU Berlin)

quotes.text: The overall computational performance of a solver crucially depends on its single constituents and the mutual interplay of these features.
The results for domain propagation surprised us.

title: Analyzing the computational impact of MIQCP solver components
contribution: The revised MIQCP component study (SCIP 2.1.1, twelve settings, written test-set rules, one job per node): eleven of twelve components help, the nonlinear ones most; binary-product reformulation should not be a default because five of eight measures degrade despite a mean-time gain.
problem_entry: As in H001: solver performance depends on its components and their interplay, and SCIP's plug-ins allow measuring each on MIQCPs (p. 3).
key_idea: Ablate one component at a time against the default (twelve settings: QCP local search added, MILP and QCP cuts separated), with relevant/control groups and per-measure better/worse marking (pp. 7–9).
assumptions: MIQCPs (quadratic objectives reformulated); 86 public instances filtered by stated rules (trivial and extremely hard removed, error cases removed, similar instances thinned out); ilaser0 excluded as wrongly answered (pp. 4, 7).

title: Comparing MIQCP solvers to a specialised algorithm for mine production scheduling
contribution: A comparison on open-pit mine production scheduling with a stockpile: general-purpose MIQCP solvers (BARON, Couenne, SBB, SCIP) run on the two formulations of a hand-crafted branch and bound come within 0.4% and 0.2% of its primal and 1.4% and 0.2% of its dual bounds on the warehouse formulation; SCIP has the best primal bounds of the global solvers.
problem_entry: General MIP solvers are hard to beat, but many nonconvex problems still need specialised algorithms: how close do generic MIQCP solvers get on a mining application the authors had worked on (pp. 3–4)?
key_idea: A head-to-head on the specialised code's own formulations (basic and warehouse), plus an a priori out-fraction discretisation tested in SCIP (pp. 6–10, 14).
assumptions: One attribute, one stockpile of infinite capacity, Assumption S; nonconvex quadratic mixing constraints; two industry instances (Marvin, 85 aggregates; Dent, 125); no public instances (pp. 5, 7–9, 13–14).
proof_devices: Mixing constraints rewritten without denominators, (14) and (19) (pp. 8–9)
The basic formulation aggregates the warehouse formulation, hence has the weaker LP relaxation (p. 10)
A priori out-fraction discretisation (20)–(23) with binary level variables (p. 10)
The benchmark's spatial branching on all aggregates at once, valid only through application knowledge (pp. 10–11)
experiments: Single-threaded Core2 Extreme X9650 3.0 GHz, 8 GB, 10,000 s; bounds and nodes at 1 h and at the end; BARON 8.1.5, Couenne 0.2, SBB (CONOPT, Ipopt), SCIP 1.1.0.11, default and written-out tuned settings; BF gaps above 57.37% for the LP-based general solvers (benchmark 13.71%); WF benchmark gaps 0.02% and 0.33%, best general primal 0.4% and 0.2% below, dual 1.4% and 0.2% away; SCIP best primal among the global solvers; 40 h SCIP runs 1.81%→1.75% and 1.08%→0.47%; discretisation beyond one level hurts (pp. 12–19).
positioning: Frames the study within the rise of general MIP solvers (Bixby et al.) and the MIP-based extensions to MINLP; the benchmark is the algorithm of Bley, Boland, Froyland and Zuckerberg from the authors' own project (pp. 3–4, 10, 12).
writing: The claim is hedged ('nearly match', 'nearly as well'); explanations are offered as intuition ('Intuitively, the reason might be'); untrusted numbers are parenthesised (pp. 3, 15, 20).
limits_future: Two instances; part of the gap from unexploited knapsack structure; only one of SCIP's 25 heuristics extended to nonlinearities; SBB only a heuristic on nonconvex problems. Future: SLP/SQP-based QCP solving in SCIP (pp. 16, 20).

title: Factorization and update of a reduced basis matrix for the revised simplex method
contribution: Forrest–Tomlin-type LU update formulas for the reduced basis matrix of basic columns and nonbasic rows, including the cases where its dimension grows or shrinks, so that a 1970s idea can run inside existing simplex codes; the benefits are argued, not measured.
problem_entry: FTRAN and BTRAN dominate simplex iterations, and the reduced-basis idea of Zoutendijk and Powell had been disregarded (pp. 3, 9).
key_idea: Factorize only A_{R̄,C} (dimension at most min{m, n}) and extend LU updates to all four basis changes, hidden behind the linear-algebra interface of existing codes (pp. 3–4, 6, 9–11).
assumptions: LP min{c'x : Ax ≥ b, x ≥ 0} for clarity; regular bases (C, R) with |C| + |R| = m; benefits greatest when bases are dominated by tight column bounds (pp. 4–5, 12).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: regularity in column form iff in row form, by a determinant identity (p. 5)
Block inverse of M giving FTRAN and BTRAN through A_{R̄,C} plus a matrix–vector product (p. 6)
Product-form updates for four basis changes; Lemma 2 for the shrinking case via deletion matrices D_j (pp. 9–10)
Forrest–Tomlin spike-and-permute for a column exchange, transposed analogue for a row exchange, bordering for growth, unit-vector replacement then deletion for shrinkage (pp. 10–11)
positioning: Revives Zoutendijk (1970) and Powell (1975), extends Forrest–Tomlin and Suhl–Suhl, unifies Nazareth's and Wunderling's column and row forms, and sets itself apart from Wunderling's 2012 kernel simplex redesign (pp. 3–4, 10–11).
writing: Advantages asserted in the abstract and introduction and argued with hedges ('may be expected') in the concluding remarks; short inline proofs (pp. 3, 5, 10, 12).
limits_future: No implementation, experiment, limitation or future work is stated (pp. 3–12).

method_links.note: computational advantages asserted in the abstract and introduction and argued in the conclusion, with no implementation or count reported; nothing missing is printed either, so Method 3 gets no ledger entry

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: revive a disregarded early idea with current machinery
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Zoutendijk's and Powell's 1970s reduced-basis idea, tested on three instances and then disregarded, restated for Forrest–Tomlin LU updates
the change hides behind the linear-algebra interface of existing simplex codes, in contrast to Wunderling's redesign; compare S054's filter around any branching rule

transferable: When an update changes a matrix's dimension, embed it in fixed-dimension updates: replace the leaving column and the entering row by unit vectors, update as for an exchange, then delete the trailing row and column of the factors (p. 11)
Exploit the block structure of the basis: factorize only the nonbasic-row × basic-column block and recover the remaining components with one matrix–vector product (p. 6)
Search the 1970s computational literature for ideas tested on a handful of instances and never adopted, and restate them for the update formulas current codes use (pp. 3–4)

quotes.text: For the next decades, however, these results have seemingly been disregarded and the idea has not been adopted by commercial simplex codes.

While he proposes to redesign the algorithmic structure of the simplex algorithm, we emphasize that the factorization of the reduced basis matrix and its update can be integrated seamlessly into existing simplex codes.

title: SCIP Optimization Suite を利用した混合整数 (線形/非線形) 計画問題の解法
contribution: A Japanese tutorial on the SCIP Optimization Suite as of SCIP 3.0 (SCIP, SoPlex, Zimpl): architecture, problem classes, interfaces, usage, debugging and testing tools, licensing, and a development roadmap that includes exact integer programming.
problem_entry: Introduce the suite and show how to model and solve MIPs and MINLPs with it (pp. 3–4).
key_idea: Plug-in architecture built on constraint handlers; branch and price via a pricer plug-in; exact rational modelling in Zimpl; SoPlex with row form and iterative refinement (pp. 5–9).
assumptions: Covers LP, MIP (with indicator and SOS constraints), MINLP (expression trees, quadratic, SOC, bivariate, absolute power), pseudo-Boolean, SAT and cumulative scheduling; more than ten file formats (pp. 5–6, 9).
proof_devices: Constraint handlers as the unit of feasibility check, propagation and separation; 126 plug-ins and 26 constraint handlers in SCIP 3.0 (p. 5)
Zimpl's exact rational arithmetic (GMP) when translating models (p. 7)
SoPlex: bound shifting instead of a phase I, Forrest–Tomlin or eta updates, row form, iterative refinement since version 1.7 (pp. 8–9)
Debug solution, debug build and test harness (p. 17)
experiments: none (illustrative runs on a 13-city TSP and stein27 only; speed claims rest on third-party benchmarks, pp. 6, 11–14)
positioning: Places SCIP in the history of LP and MIP (Dantzig, Gomory, Land–Doig), the MIPLIB 2010 speed-up record and CP–SAT–MIP integration; Zimpl against commercial modelling languages such as gams and ampl (pp. 3–4, 7).

title: Undercover Branching
contribution: Undercover branching: restrict branching candidates to a minimum cover of the MINLP whenever the candidate set meets it; the rule changes decisions on 23 of 195 MINLPLib instances, where it solves two more instances and cuts shifted geometric mean time by 79% (reliability rule) and 76% (pseudocost rule).
problem_entry: Branching drives MIP performance, yet MINLP branching mostly adopts MIP rules and ignores the nonlinearity when branching on fractional integer variables (pp. 3–5).
key_idea: A global, exactly computed minimum cover as a pre-selection filter over any variable-based branching rule, computed once, without sampling, restarts or strict priorities (pp. 5, 8–9).
assumptions: MINLP (1) with constraint functions twice continuously differentiable on the box interior; Theorem 1 (covers are the vertex covers of the co-occurrence graph), Corollary 1 (NP-hard), Lemma 1 (an integer cover with finite bounds gives at most ∏(u_i − ℓ_i + 1) MIPs); 195 of 273 MINLPLib instances after named removals (pp. 5–6, 8–10).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: cover iff vertex cover of the co-occurrence graph of the Hessian sparsity (proof in [10]) (p. 6)
Corollary 1 by reduction from vertex cover (p. 6)
Lemma 1: enumeration bound for an integer cover (p. 8)
Pre-selection algorithm wrapping branch_int and branch_spat (Fig. 2, p. 8)
experiments: SCIP 3.0 with CPLEX 12.4, CppAD and Ipopt 3.10.2; Xeon X5672 3.2 GHz, 1 h, Hyperthreading and Turboboost off, one job per node; Undercover heuristic and restarts off; How often: 23 of 195 affected; How good: two more solved per base rule, shifted geometric means (shifts 100 nodes, 100 strong branchings, 10 s) −79% time, −52% nodes, −45% strong branches (reliability/pseudocost) and −76% time, −45% nodes (pseudocost/pseudocost); losses counted; robust to removing three outliers (pp. 9–13).
positioning: Set against pseudocost, strong, reliability and hybrid branching, information-based branching (Kılınç Karzan et al.), backdoor branching (Fischetti and Monaci), violation transfer (Tawarmalani and Sahinidis) and pseudocosts for continuous variables (Belotti et al.); builds on the Undercover heuristic (pp. 4–5).
writing: Two questions as subsection titles; hopes stated as hopes ('our hope', 'This result is not overly surprising'); two text–table slips in the result paragraph, one repeated in the conclusion (pp. 10–13).
limits_future: Only 23 of 195 instances affected. Future: non-minimum covers and the cover-size trade-off; detect linear subproblems with large subtrees and give them to a pure MIP solver (p. 13).
